close_rendering: The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not lack.
whats_happening: The psalm opens by naming a relation and then stating what follows from it, in four Hebrew words with no verb joining the first two. The line is built as two halves, and almost everything the psalm goes on to say is an unpacking of the first half. The word rendered my shepherd is not a noun but a participle, so the claim is about something God is doing rather than a title God holds.

key_words.note: A participle in construct with a first person suffix, so closer to the one shepherding me than to a fixed title.
The verb is about lacking or coming up short, not about desiring.

translation_note: Older English versions render the second half I shall not want, using want in its older sense of lack. The Hebrew verb concerns shortage, not appetite, which is why modern versions move away from want.

claims.claim: רֹעִי is a Qal active participle, masculine singular, in construct with a first person singular suffix.
אֶחְסָר is a Qal imperfect, first person singular.
No verb joins יְהוָה to רֹעִי in the first half of the line.
The Masoretic text counts the superscription מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד inside verse 1, where English versification places it before the numbered verse.

evidence.note: OSHB marks the English verse boundary with an inline note, KJV:Ps.23.1

claims.claim: The verse opens a six-verse psalm running to Psalm 23:6.
Shepherd was a widely used image for a king or a deity in the ancient Near East.
What time frame the imperfect אֶחְסָר carries is disputed.

positions.label: Future
positions.case: The Hebrew imperfect commonly carries future reference, which makes the line a statement of confidence about what is to come rather than a report of present circumstances.

positions.label: General present
positions.case: The imperfect also expresses habitual or characteristic action, which makes the line a statement about how things stand generally, matching the settled tone of the psalm's remaining verses.

related_passages.note: The shepherd image is unpacked into specific actions.
God as shepherd set against the failed shepherds of Israel.
The good shepherd saying takes up the same image.
